questions.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

I. ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}]$

II. ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{aligned}]$

III. ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{aligned}]$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6u+3v \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}|=5\cdot 6-3\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=4\cdot (-3)-(-4)\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot (-6)-(-4)\cdot 8=-10\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{3}$ only."

questions.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=4u+2v-5,\,y=2u+v+6.
$$

Suppose that $A$ is the matrix that represents the linear transformation associated with $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]$

II. $det(A)=0$

III. The transformation is invertible
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4u+2v-5 \\ 2u+v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4u+2v \\ 2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\ne [\begin{aligned}4 & -5 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 4-2\cdot 2=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $det(A)=0,$ the affine transformation is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5u-2v-5 \\ 10u-4v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5u-2v \\ 10u-4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{aligned}|=-4\cdot 5-(-2)\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-4 \\ u+5v+7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}|=5\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 1=6\ne 0.

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}|=6\cdot 2-4\cdot 3=0.

questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ -2u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2)=9\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u+v \\ 4u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u \\ 8u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot 1-0\cdot 8=7.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

questions.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & 5 \\ b & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}c \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 7-(-5)\cdot (4)}[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 4 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=3+4+3=10.
$$

$$

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{5\cdot (-5)-6\cdot (-4)}[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v-4,\,y=2u-4v-5.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+ay+b,\,v=x-y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v-4 \\ 2u-4v-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\ 2u-4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+4 \\ y+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+4)+(-\frac{3}{2})\cdot (y+5) \\ 1\cdot (x+4)+(-1)\cdot (y+5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{3}{2}y+\frac{1}{2} \\ x-y-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+(-\frac{3}{2})y+\frac{1}{2},\,v=x-y+(-1).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+(-1)=-2.
$$

\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2v-4 \\ u+4v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2v \\ u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+4 \\ y-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+4)+1\cdot (y-6) \\ (-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (x+4)+0\cdot (y-6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x+y+2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}x-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+2,\,v=(-\frac{1}{2})x+0y-2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+(-\frac{1}{2})+0=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is a zero matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the triangle under the action of $T$ is a point on the plane.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = u - v - 2, \qquad y = v - u + 5.
$$

Suppose that $A$ is the matrix representing the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/44640c1fb1ad0e508361835195c5905aa0f8b96fea7441946af82f5502a1fe1f.svg)

II. $\det(A) = 0$

III. The transformation is invertible
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-2 \\ v-u+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ -u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/316e64a93b5994c4ffded0e97ccf35fcee0d4645edcf03053258b12373d75f14.svg)

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/458a4a97aaad6b0a58b5f567b1110b6e412ce80b087698bc1cdf89cab4db6aa7.svg)

- Statement III is false. Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the affine transformation is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Example: 
                    Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Matrix Form
canonical_examples.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/2d764b0ce2b8e459df02d2982e3e720531ac14b6e7a557be2439d705687daf8d.svg)

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/0129c63040aaf2bb5328a5503ad530ae4d4007ed127da5459ffb9412f87bd24c.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $\mathbf T$ gives us the following information:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/8c2634c13ae57aca4e0b44aee83be721fa2c794a4e5207e01f98ec4e9f37f01a.svg)

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 7-(-9)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = -7 + 3 + 8 = 4.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form
canonical_examples.problem:
The affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is defined as

$$
x = u - v + 2, \qquad y = 4u - 5v + 9.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ of $\mathbf T$ is

$$
u = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{a}x - y + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{b}, \qquad v = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{c}x - y + 1,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+2 \\ 4u-5v+9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ 4u-5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-5)-(-1)\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y-9) \\ 4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y-9)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5x-y-1 \\ 4x-y+1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{5}x - y + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{(-1)}, \qquad v = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{4}x - y + 1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = 5 + (-1) + 4 = 8.
$$

                    Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/8797a50ddc0750a97190f96d8bc1cffe70c6ef9cc8e55a46f5a75d6b6702c81d.png)

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/ebe616d2801c2fb5cc444dabff8490f1940e4b8695f2ef8188796cac8a011427.svg) 
Describe the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/647f222d22618200ce471fd9c65605f8c5400423b28a98a7bb3797c0f31617e6.svg)

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-4\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is non-invertible and the image of the triangle under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. The **inverse** of $\mathbf T$ (if it exists) is an affine transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ such that

$$
\mathbf T^{-1} (\mathbf T(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf T (\mathbf T^{-1}(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf u
$$

for every vector $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2.$ In other words, the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ reverses the action of $\mathbf T.$ 

Not all affine transformations are invertible. So how can we determine whether a given affine transformation is invertible?

To answer this, recall that an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ can be expressed in matrix form as

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. We can reverse the action of $\mathbf T$ by making $\mathbf u$ the subject of this equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ {A}^{-1}\cdot Au & ={A}^{-1}\cdot (x-b) \\ {I}_{2}\cdot u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b) \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b)\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives us a method of computing the inverse of an affine transformation. Additionally, we have the following:

*An affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is invertible if and only if the matrix $A$ that represents the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is invertible, that is, $\det(A) \neq 0.$*

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/612bd57a16c06b8648edea514a060dc06ec6d9cd61486882209101c1d626d2ea.svg)

We wish to determine whether $\mathbf T^{-1}$ exists and find its matrix form if it does exist. 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/aebda34312bb6625d26bdafce97790a9c48334113b1b83912117811672e5680e.svg)

Since $\det(A) \neq 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible. 

To compute the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ we will use the formula we derived earlier:

$$
\mathbf{u} = A^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})
$$

We start by calculating the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix form of the inverse affine transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: Finding the Inverse of an Affine Transformation
tutorials.content:
Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ expressed in matrix form as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/612bd57a16c06b8648edea514a060dc06ec6d9cd61486882209101c1d626d2ea.svg)

We wish to determine whether $\mathbf T^{-1}$ exists and find its matrix form if it does exist. 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/aebda34312bb6625d26bdafce97790a9c48334113b1b83912117811672e5680e.svg)

Since $\det(A) \neq 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible. 

To compute the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ we will use the formula we derived earlier:

$$
\mathbf{u} = A^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})
$$

We start by calculating the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix form of the inverse affine transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Image Types Formed by Affine Transformations
tutorials.problem:
Consider the square in the $uv$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/a8cc0923da86a1a1ac6b666893397263ef3865448080500caa6f17510547d901.png)

We wish to explore the image of this square under an affine transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors.

Similar to linear transformations, there are three possibilities depending on the value of $\det(A)$.

- $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular ($\det(A)\neq 0$). In this case, our square is mapped to a parallelogram.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/e4efbdf8bf71fbd3f5df1c8c15f8ab07f2141e4cac85ddfebda6ddb1f72908c7.svg) 
Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane, we get the following parallelogram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/36da067393fa53f4296373d65e3c6177a54d1a901824188687b4a74ea171afdf.png)

- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ has at least one nonzero entry. In this case, our square is mapped to a line segment.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/e7a9bb24dd89f58158c51cec1d659a5dd209543ec69950ee176ca59955ee4b72.svg) 
Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following line segment:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/5e5481e5b2f2218a6097020e260dc991cde05574372c724aa07527458257d94c.png)

- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ is the zero matrix. In this case, our square is mapped to a point on the plane.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/1c5397ef65390e44112c66c22d1b12b74d591c464fd62d2dfd6243983a480df0.svg) 
Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/0072c5e06674f79f82e771744fda217e6558830f7a6e4ab387aa9dbf4dda09bc.png)

tutorials.title: Image Types Formed by Affine Transformations
tutorials.content:
Consider the square in the $uv$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/a8cc0923da86a1a1ac6b666893397263ef3865448080500caa6f17510547d901.png)

We wish to explore the image of this square under an affine transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors.

Similar to linear transformations, there are three possibilities depending on the value of $\det(A)$.

- $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular ($\det(A)\neq 0$). In this case, our square is mapped to a parallelogram.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/e4efbdf8bf71fbd3f5df1c8c15f8ab07f2141e4cac85ddfebda6ddb1f72908c7.svg) 
Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane, we get the following parallelogram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/36da067393fa53f4296373d65e3c6177a54d1a901824188687b4a74ea171afdf.png)

- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ has at least one nonzero entry. In this case, our square is mapped to a line segment.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/e7a9bb24dd89f58158c51cec1d659a5dd209543ec69950ee176ca59955ee4b72.svg) 
Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following line segment:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/5e5481e5b2f2218a6097020e260dc991cde05574372c724aa07527458257d94c.png)

- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ is the zero matrix. In this case, our square is mapped to a point on the plane.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/1c5397ef65390e44112c66c22d1b12b74d591c464fd62d2dfd6243983a480df0.svg) 
Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274045/assets/0072c5e06674f79f82e771744fda217e6558830f7a6e4ab387aa9dbf4dda09bc.png)

tutorials.name: A Summary of Image Types
tutorials.problem:
In general, if we consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the mapping

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, then we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases: 

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane (namely, the point with position vector $\mathbf b$).
